title: Adjustment En Route to Everest
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Opening his 2022 blogging year, Stuart addresses the frustration teachers feel when years of study and adjustment still don't make the work of teaching easy. He offers a geometric reframe: when you aim at something as far off as students' long-term flourishing through mastery of disciplines with millennia of accrued complexity, hitting that target with a perfectly straight line is essentially impossible, so ongoing course correction is a built-in feature of the goal, not evidence of failure. He pairs this with a personal anecdote about driving toward Mount Denali, where the mountain was visible at first but repeatedly obscured by trees, hills, and weather along the route — a metaphor for how the ascent itself can obscure the destination even when the initial course was sound. He closes by naming the tension between staying a previously chosen course and adjusting it as a genuine judgment call, calling the ability to discern between the two 'one of the first fruits of wisdom.'
points: Stuart's core reframe treats the need for constant adjustment not as a sign of doing it wrong, but as a geometric inevitability of aiming at any sufficiently distant, ambitious goal.

The Denali anecdote supplies a concrete image for a common but hard-to-articulate experience: the destination is visible at times and obscured at others, even while the traveler stays on a sound course.

He explicitly resists collapsing 'stay the course' and 'adjust the course' into a single rule, instead naming the tension between them as an ongoing judgment call requiring wisdom rather than formula.
By opening the new year with this piece, Stuart frames struggle and recalibration as expected companions to any Everest-level goal like students' long-term flourishing, not signs the goal was wrong.
quotes: Everest-level goals guarantee the need for course correction. When we pick something to aim at that's far off — something like the long-term flourishing of young people via teaching them to master disciplines with thousands of years of accrued complexity — we're bound to need course corrections as we go.
It's just geometry. When you start at one point and you aim at another that's far away, the likelihood of being able to hit the far away point with a perfectly straight line is really low.
Mastery is an ongoing process — not a checklist or a test at the end of a unit. Doesn't mean get rid of tests or checklists. It just means, this is hard.

I imagine hiking and climbing a great peak is similar. You don't always see clearly where you're heading. Sometimes, the ascent obscures the summit. But the successful mountaineer maintains the course that they intelligently selected when the view was clear.

There's a time to stay the course you previously set, and there's a time to adjust because the course you previously set isn't going to arrive where you want it to. One of the first fruits of wisdom is knowing when to do what.
